tagline: A forested Divide crossing links mining towns and cliff dwellings.
intro: Trail of the Mountain Spirits winds across the forested Continental Divide in southwestern New Mexico, linking mining towns and the Gila country. New Mexico’s tourism department presents the National Scenic Byway as a route through six climatic zones, with cliff dwellings and year-round birding. The Federal Highway Administration allows three hours to drive it, or six to eight hours to explore. The state calls it the Inner Loop, a name associated with the annual Tour of the Gila bicycle race. NM 15 winds north from Silver City toward the monument; its final approach passes Gila Hot Springs in the valley of the Gila River’s West Fork.

The Gila’s history includes a deliberate limit on road building. In 1922, Forest Service supervisor Aldo Leopold proposed protecting the river’s headwaters by excluding roads and denying use permits. His work led to recognition of the Gila as the National Forest System’s first wilderness area in 1924. The cliff dwellings monument adjoins that wilderness.

Start in Silver City and head north toward Pinos Altos, then continue to Gila Hot Springs and the cliff dwellings at the end of NM 15. Return for the loop through Mimbres on NM 35, then turn west toward Santa Rita’s copper mine. The return passes Santa Clara, where US 180 leads west to Silver City.

moments.title: Pinos Altos
moments.text: Pinos Altos takes its name from tall pines that were cut down as the mining town grew. Gold discovered in the nearby mountains brought the town into being in 1860. It was first called Birchville after Robert H. Birch, one of the three discoverers. The population reached about 9,000 during the 1880s and 1890s before the town slowly emptied in the early 1900s. George Hearst invested in local mines and built a stamp mill here in 1889. Many original buildings remain, and the former mining town now has summer homes and serves tourists.

moments.title: Gila Cliff Dwellings National Monument
moments.text: The Mogollon builders used five natural cliff alcoves above Cliff Dweller Canyon to make connected dwellings. Archaeologists have identified 46 rooms. Tree-ring dating places the cutting of the buildings’ wood between 1276 and 1287. Why the community left is unknown. In 1906, Gila Forest Supervisor R. C. McClure called for federal protection to prevent further artifact removal; the monument was established the following year. The dwellings are reached by a one-mile loop trail with footbridges over a stream. The surrounding country has steep-sided canyons, with ponderosa pine and Gambel’s oak among the trees on its mesas and bluffs.

moments.title: Chino Mine
moments.text: Santa Rita’s copper pit expanded into the space occupied by its town. Mining in the area began late in the Spanish colonial period. Early in the nineteenth century, crudely smelted ore went to Chihuahua for further processing, then traveled to Mexico City by mule. Open-pit expansion later forced Santa Rita to move repeatedly. After a move in 1957, heavy rain washed mud and boulders into the new townsite. Santa Rita was abandoned in 1967. The area’s school system continued until 1972, five years after the town’s abandonment. Chino remains an open-pit copper mine, while Santa Rita is a ghost town.
